summary.text: Nucleic acids are large molecules found in all cells and viruses, built as chains of nucleotides.
The two main kinds are DNA and RNA, told apart by their sugar: deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA.
They carry information in cells and both play a crucial role in directing protein synthesis.

items.prompt: A lab sample's chains contain thymine but no uracil. What does that tell you?

options.label: It is RNA, since thymine is an RNA base
It is DNA, since thymine occurs only there
It is neither, since nucleic acids lack thymine
It could be either, since both use thymine equally

items.explain: Thymine occurs only in DNA and uracil only in RNA, so thymine without uracil points to DNA.

items.prompt: You break a nucleic acid chain into its repeating units. What does each unit contain?

options.label: A 5-carbon sugar, an amino acid and a nitrogenous base
A 6-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a fatty acid
A phosphate group, an amino acid and a fatty acid
A 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base

items.explain: Nucleic acids are made of nucleotides, and each nucleotide is a 5-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.

items.prompt: Nearly all living cells hold both kinds of nucleic acid. What is usual for a virus?

options.label: It holds one kind in its genome, usually not both
It holds both kinds, just as cells do
It holds neither, since viruses have no nucleic acid
It holds only the double-stranded kind, never single

items.explain: Viruses contain either DNA or RNA, but usually not both.

items.prompt: Why are these molecules called nucleic acids?

options.label: They neutralize the acids found inside the cell nucleus
First found in blood, and they contain nitrogen only
First found in the nucleus, and they contain acidic phosphate groups
They dissolve the nucleus whenever a cell divides

items.explain: They were named for their discovery within the nucleus and for their phosphate groups, which relate to phosphoric acid.

items.prompt: You compare the usual natural shapes of the two main nucleic acids. What do you find?

options.label: DNA has one strand; RNA has two strands
Both usually have two strands
Both usually have one strand
DNA has two strands; RNA has one strand

items.explain: In most cases naturally occurring DNA is double-stranded and RNA is single-stranded, though there are exceptions.

items.prompt: What did the Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment demonstrate?

options.label: That DNA carries genetic information
That DNA has a double-helix shape
That DNA contains the base uracil
That DNA is made only of sugar

items.explain: The 1944 experiment showed DNA is the carrier of genetic information; the double helix was proposed later by Watson and Crick.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of nucleic acid
paragraphs.text: DNA and RNA are the two main classes of nucleic acid. Their full names are deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid. Nucleic acids are big biomolecules, and every cell and virus depends crucially on them. Inside cells they hold information and form the genetic material, and both DNA and RNA play a crucial part in directing how proteins are made.

paragraphs.heading: Built from nucleotides
paragraphs.text: A nucleic acid is a linear polymer, a chain, of units called nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a sugar with five carbons, a phosphate group that makes the molecule acidic, and a nitrogenous base. The base together with the sugar is called a nucleoside. Along the chain, sugars and phosphates alternate, joined by phosphodiester linkages, to form the sugar-phosphate backbone.

paragraphs.heading: Telling them apart
paragraphs.text: The sugar decides which one you have. A chain built on ribose is RNA, while a chain built on deoxyribose, a variant of ribose, is DNA; the two sugars differ only by a hydroxyl group. The bases differ too. Adenine, cytosine and guanine show up in both, but thymine is limited to DNA, and uracil to RNA. In most natural cases DNA is double-stranded and RNA single-stranded, though some viruses have double-stranded RNA or single-stranded DNA genomes.

paragraphs.heading: Carrying information
paragraphs.text: The order of the bases is what carries the information. In DNA, the sequence of base pairs helps store and pass on coded instructions as genes. In RNA, the sequence helps make new proteins, which determine most chemical processes of living things. All living cells hold both DNA and RNA, apart from some such as mature red blood cells, while viruses usually hold one or the other.

paragraphs.heading: Giant molecules
paragraphs.text: Nucleic acids are usually very large. DNA molecules are probably the biggest single molecules known. Well-studied examples run from small interfering RNA, just 21 nucleotides long, up to whole chromosomes. Human chromosome 1 is one single molecule containing 247 million base pairs.

paragraphs.heading: How they were found
paragraphs.text: Friedrich Miescher made a first, partial discovery of nucleic acid in 1869 at the University of Tübingen, Germany, and called his new substance nuclein. In the early 1880s Albrecht Kossel purified it further, found it was highly acidic, and later identified the bases. Richard Altmann coined the term nucleic acid in 1889. The name comes from the nucleus, where these acids were first found, and from their phosphate groups. DNA was shown to carry genetic information by the Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment of 1944, and in 1953 Watson and Crick proposed its double-helix structure.
